Mr. Speaker, there is no denying that I too agree with this bill which was introduced by my government when it was in power. I am pleased to see that the minister is here. I should like to open a new bracket concerning this Customs Tariff Act. In the riding I represent, that of Argenteuil, we find the largest airport in North America, that of Mirabel. On rereading this bill, I decided to speak to this House of a problem that exists at Mirabel but that could easily be solved. It would be very easy to do if the minister decided to make of Mirabel a free port where primary products would be taken, processed then exported to the United States where we would have a market of over $200 million. It is most important to realize that such a project would be a first in North America; this type of thing does exist only in a few countries where what is commonly known as "duty-free zones" have been developed-

-where the manufacturing and assembly processes could be created in order to expand our market to our neighbours, the United States. We have in this country, especially in the riding of Argenteuil, the necessary manpower and technology. The only thing we would need is the facility through an amendment to the customs law.

It would be a cinch considering there already is on the Mirabel property the infrastructure of an industrial park, access to the specialized work force of the neighbouring automobile industry in the riding of my colleague from Blain-ville-Deux-Montagnes; and then I see the list of material to which these amendments will apply: typewriters, phonographs, record players, cameras. In short, all that is being amended by this bill could easily be assembled within a duty-free zone; and when 1 say that, Mr. Speaker, I merely mean an area in which primary goods could be imported duty free, assembled there and then exported to another country.
Argenteuil has numerous advantages and, of course, our friends the Tories have always called Mirabel "a white elephant" but nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, it exists. It is there and it will not disappear. We might as well stop politicking and make out of it something that will benefit all the population of my constituency. Close to Mirabel, you have the city of Lachute where many businesses had to close down for various

November 5, 1979
Customs Tariff
reasons. Here again, Mr. Speaker, we find a demographic concentration that could benefit from a duty-free zone for assembling and manufacturing factories, which could be easily established. I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) will take this statement under consideration and remember that his Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) often says the time has come for action.
The Tory government can now use this tool to act, and I think that this amendment to the Customs tariff should include a provision to make Mirabel a duty-free zone in order to aid Quebec manufacturers and others who may want to settle in this region which is full of opportunities for industry and a population who would certainly welcome this move.
This bill includes provisions on vegetables. Market gardening is very important in the area surrounding the Argenteuil riding, and the eastern part of the riding as well as the Deux-Montagnes area are great apple producers. This could lead to a canning industry for export which would also benefit the area.
The object of this amendment would be to create jobs for the population of Argenteuil, the population of Quebec, in this year when we need a most comprehensive attitude from the government.
[ Translation]
Not only is it very important to deal with an issue such as this, but I suggest that the present government should give top priority to the industrial and commercial development of Mirabel. Enough with all these demands. We must live with an elephant, Mr. Speaker, and it is the taxpayers of the whole of Canada who must assume the costs of its maintenance.
To those who blame the previous government, 1 can reply that 1 had no part in it. But they will not be able to blame me for not doing my duty and failing to urge the House to create an industrial region which would include the Mirabel area, in order to create the many jobs which are required in the Argenteuil riding where the rate of unemployment can reach 33 per cent during certain periods of the year. That is the reason for my insistence, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that the minister and his parliamentary secretary will look into this problem which Quebec is now facing. This is of utmost importance, Mr. Speaker, since we all seem to agree to this legislation, so that the minister may introduce his budget in the House as soon as possible.
During the months preceding the election I have seen our Tory friends opposite criticizing the budget tabled by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) and saying how bad it was that such a budget be supported by a government. Maybe it is due to my naivete or my lack of experience, Mr. Speaker, but 1 do not understand why the Minister of Finance now sitting in this House cannot bring in a budget some six

months after having assumed that position. What is he waiting for? Or is it that the budget brought down by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice was so good, and 1 believe it was, that he is simply going to carry on with the budget presented by the former minister of finance.
I will now conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by renewing my request for his department as well as the Department of National Revenue to study seriously the matter 1 have raised and I hope that during the coming sessions we will have opportunities to discuss it more thoroughly and that very soon the ministers concerned will be in a position to transform the expropriated area of Mirabel into a duty-free zone to help the manufacturers who want to export and assemble goods in Quebec and especially in Argenteuil.

As Mr. Speaker is aware, second reading of a bill was devised to discuss the principle of a particular bill. 1 would suggest that discussions which range all over the atmosphere, all over right field and left field in second reading of a bill, are not only incorrect but accomplish really nothing.
There are two principles in which I am very interested in regard to this particular bill. Imports have a place, but when we are talking about tariffs and the farmers of this country, whether it is for fruits, vegetables or anything else, the major principle which must be considered is: How does it affect producers? When we provide tariffs which will destroy industry inside our country, certainly we are doing our producers no good whatsoever.
Over the years we have seen situations where imports have made it almost impossible, if not impossible, for producers in the country to produce. That is why so many of them have gone under during the last ten years. Any law pertaining to producers should ensure that the tariffs will not destroy or injure the Canadian production of foods. If we keep that point in mind, ensure that Canadian producers have a fair show in producing, and then provide them with a reasonable return for their production, we will be amazed at what can be produced in Canada through the use of hothouse agricultural technology, etc.
The second principle is: How does it affect the consumer? When we raise tariffs and leave them on continually, so that during the last two or three winters the people of this country had to pay $1 a head for lettuce, they are certainly not accomplishing their purpose. Not only is it inflationary, but it is causing consumers either to go without or is providing lettuce only for those who have plenty of cash. That is not the purpose of a tariff. I believe the purpose of a tariff should be to give producers a chance and an incentive to produce. Also it should provide as fair a price as possible to the consumers of these important products. If our tariffs accomplish these two principles, we will see a thriving industry in the country and we will ensure that our consumers get the food they require to build strong, healthy bodies.
November 5, 1979

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate which I think is the second one that can be called a liberal measure; for example, on the 22nd you vote "blue". All Quebeckers remember that famous slogan of Mr. Andre Payette who is now I believe the Prime Minister's adviser on public relations and who was at that time in the advertising business and was interviewing a lady buying her groceries. She was flabbergasted by food prices and was saying; Mr. Payette, the only solution 1 see to those prices is to vote "blue" on the 22nd. Some Canadians believed it more than I would have liked, and finally, on the 22nd, they voted "blue"to give us that government opposite, that government which in spite of its many promises, introduces a Liberal legislation.
Like my colleague from Windsor West, 1 support this legislation because it was first introduced by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) in a budget beneficial to all Canadians; but 1 am outraged that this government was not more original and did not introduce its own legislation.
i am pleased that consumers will be protected against overly massive imports of foreign products. Farmers in my riding will also be protected. Potatoes, strawberries and other fruit and vegetable growers in my riding will have access to the Canadian market at a better price for Canadian consumers. The advertising of the Progressive Conservative Party might have been dishonest or misleading, and perhaps the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) should set up an inquiry and at the same time look at the embassy issue.
On the night of May 22, the people in my riding were very disappointed to see that a Progressive Conservative government was in power, but they thought: With all their promises, they will certainly introduce legislation to help us, especially as concerns food costs, since even the commercials named the guilty party. Most Quebeckers saw this. The former prime minister was to blame for the increase in the price of bread and for everything else.
Now 1 am wondering whether we are making this government guilty of plagiarism. During the campaign, they had answers for everything, and now their only answer is to salvage the Liberal solutions. All members of my party and myself will support this because we hope it will help the Canadian producer and give some respite to the consumer.
However, Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I am extremely disappointed because even though 1 did not have any confidence in this government, I thought that they must have something ready to suggest in view of all the promises that they were making.
In this case, for instance, we see that they want to help reduce horticultural imports. They had also promised to do the same for dairy products. Since this subject is not covered by Bill C-18,1 hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), in co-operation with his colleagues, will succeed in reducing
Customs Tariff
imports in this area. The government wanted to stop importing cheese and other food products. As a matter of fact, one of their famous promises was on this subject.
They have not found anything better to suggest than the Liberal proposals. I had to smile when I read in one of the schedules of the bill the reference to the import of coffins. 1 invite Parliament to pass this bill as soon as possible in case the government itself needs a coffin after tomorrow evening.
I have nothing to add and I wish only to remind the government that the motto of Quebeckers is; "Je me souviens" and that we remember those famous promises, that famous commercial and we shall not forget it for quite some time. I hope that at the time of the coming budget, should the government last until then, we shall be able to judge its performance. Mr. Payette, who did a commercial with so much verve might use a little more verve to try and convince his leader to participate more actively in the referendum debate.
Mr. Speaker, those were the few remarks I had to make on the subject. We shall ask more detailed questions when studying the bill clause by clause.

Mr. Speaker, I am amused by the discussions that are taking place under this old ways and means motion contained in Bill C-18. 1 was particularly amused by the remarks of the hon. member who preceded me and who said "Je me souviens". They remember whatever the hell they want, and they forget whatever they don't want to remember.
Cheese was mentioned, but I point out that this problem did not exist until the former prime minister went to Europe and made a deal for gradual entry into the common market, establishing what is called a shoulder to shoulder sort of relationship. He made that deal and the price was the entry of 45 million pounds. That was the price of that deal. Hon. members remember what they want to remember and forget what they do not want to remember. I suppose that is always the case.
One of the problems we have with this kind of a bill is that it does not say anything or it says everything, depending on how you interpret it. It has become a means by which people speak in favour of high tariffs or recommend free tariffs. I suppose civil servants who understand something about tariff practice know what is being done, but 1 am sure most members of Parliament cannot understand these ways and means motions, how these things come about, or what the situation was before amendment. I can read as well as anyone and I would be quite happy to refer to some of the items.
A previous speaker mentioned lettuce and suggested that if it were not for the tariff structure we would not be paying high prices in the wintertime. It is indicated that the tariff on lettuce is 85 cents a pound, which I think is high, or free. It is free in any 12-month period ending March 31. It states that it shall not be maintained in force in excess of 16 weeks, which

November 5, 1979
Customs Tariff
may be divided into two separate periods, and the free rate shall apply whenever the specific duty is not in effect. In other words, it does not apply throughout the year. So the tariff is not really the reason for these high prices, except during those periods when Canadians are producing either at the beginning or at the end of the season.
We have before us a bill that the minister has said he will favour, support and endorse. He did not go so far as to say that he was going to understand it. Most ways and means motions introduced in this House leave a lot to be desired. We have references to South Africa and whether we should maintain the preferential treatment which was extended in 1932. We have heard about other arrangements which were made many years ago, and some references to whether we should now accept or continue those arrangements. The bill does not say what those arrangements were, it does not include an explanation of them and it does not indicate what are the recommended changes. In fact, the words in the ways and means motion only relate to changes that are going to take place.
In relation to the New Zealand agreement of 1932 clause 11 says that we will strike out tariff items 104a and 106 and the enumerations of goods and the rates of duties set opposite each of those items. Then it goes on to say that any enactment founded upon the motion shall be deemed to have come into effect on October 24 and to have applied to all goods mentioned in the said motion imported or taken out of the warehouse, and so on. There are another two or three lines that do not mean any more than the lines to which I have just referred. Then the bill goes on to provide much the same things for Australia and South Africa.
The Australian trade agreement goes back to 1960, but the South African trade agreement goes back to 1932. The members of this Parliament are being asked either to pass this bill or turn it down. If we pass the bill, what have we done to our agreements with New Zealand, Australia, or South Africa? I imagine there are very few people on the tariff board who know what is mentioned in the original agreement. If the government wishes to amend an act, it should at least give the section. I probably have the 1960 amendments in my office, but I do not believe that any member, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), would have the amendment which was negotiated in 1932.
It is in his head.

It may be in his head. He has just arrived and he can give that information himself. However, I do not think that it is in this bill, and how can we make even small changes to a tariff agreement with another country that was negotiated in 1932 or, for that matter, in 1960, when the government does not give the sections of the act that it is amending? I do not think that it matters one way or another. It has not really made a great deal of difference to anyone as to what happens with regard to tariff adjustments. These adjustments have
[Mr. Peters.)
been made many times, and there are always changes indicated in the ways and means motions.
In the agricultural field, however, there are too many problems which are of an immediate nature and which can have a detrimental and catastrophic effect on farmers of various commodities. The soft fruit industry has almost entirely disappeared from Canada, such fruits as peaches, cherries and strawberries. Most of the fruit industry in Ontario has disappeared simply because it could not compete in world markets. As I understand it, most of us in this House would like to have free trade and believe that it is a wonderful thing, provided it does not affect our commodities. Naturally, we want to protect our commodities, and I suppose that is true of every business from the peach producer to automobile manufacturer.
But what has happened? Certainly you, Mr. Speaker, have had personal contact with this situation and are aware of the inability of the trade board to operate fast enough to provide the kind of protection necessary with regard to agricultural commodities. It is interesting to note that in all these changes the tariff only applies to a specific field when it comes to agricultural products. The tariff is applied in the period when the surplus in another country is at its peak and our system is either beginning or ending, in most cases beginning.
This prevents countries with which Canada does not have anti-dumping laws from dumping in our country during our peak periods. They would normally be in a position to dump their agricultural products in Canada at the beginning of our season when production costs are still very high and the production period has not yet begun. The government is allowed to make these changes. If one were to take any commodity, and I will use cauliflower as an example, free rates shall apply during the months of January, February, March, April and May. I presume that is because our storage facilities will not hold cauliflower over a longer period. During the remaining months, however, in any 12-month period ending March 31, the specific duty or ad valorem duty, as the case may be, shall not be maintained in force in excess of 20 weeks, which may be divided into two separate periods, and the free rate shall apply whenever the specific duty or ad valorem duty is not in effect.
The reason for 20 weeks is that that is our period of production. We have always found, whether it be cauliflower, cherries or any other commodity, that the tariff board never reacts quickly enough to protect the farmer. The farmer is the victim of the improper or slow use of the regulatory tool with regard to applying tariffs. There may be one or two reasons for this. One may be that the government wants to make money, and they may be able to collect more money from the tariff than from their share of the production. I presume that this is true with regard to many of the commodities in Canada.
The Department of Agriculture does not have a say as to when the tariff shall apply. This means that by the time the matter has gone through two or three departments the problem has developed to a stage where the tariff will no longer alleviate the problem. This was found to be the case with imported meats. For a long time offshore meats were imported
November 5, 1979

into Canada at a rate which was considerably below what the Canadian market could stand. Boxed meat was being brought in from Australia and South America, and this constituted unfair competition to the meat producers in Canada, which meant that the price of beef was depressed for a considerable period of time.
When supplies of this offshore meat dried up, Canadian producers could not meet the demand and consequently the price jumped, which was a great detriment to the consumer because of the advantages taken by the importers and those in the wholesale meat business. That situation could have been balanced out to the best advantage of both the consumer and the producer. The producer would not have been subjected to the low prices then and would not have experienced the difficulties created in a market where the price to the consumer was too high.
One of the reasons that we have had so much difficulty with agricultural production is simply that the Department of Agriculture has not had the mechanism to control agricultural structures and has had no way of applying these tariffs at the most opportune moment. 1 am not suggesting that there is anything wrong with these tariffs or the periods which are mentioned in the bill. It may well be that 30 weeks is the right amount of time for cabbage because cabbage keeps a lot longer than cauliflower. It may well be that 20 weeks is long enough for cauliflower.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may we discuss motion No. 7? May we, with the unanimous consent of the House, stand motions Nos. 3 and 5?

Is it
agreed that we stand these two items?
Agreed.

That a special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs be established to monitor the government's progress on the implementation of the recommendations of the previous subcommittee on penitentiaries, and to conduct such further inquiries and to travel as may be required.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as indicated in the notice of motion, the purpose of the motion this afternoon, which I hope will receive consent on all sides of the House, is basically to revive the terms of reference of a subcommittee established on October 21, 1976, well over three years ago. The reason for the notice of motion is that, despite the fact that the subcommittee had extensive meetings and came up with a unanimous report, today far too many of the recommendations of the subcommittee have yet to be implemented.
As 1 have indicated, it was on October 21, 1976, that the original subcommittee was established with consent from all sides of this House. I think it is important to indicate to the House that one of the reasons for that was that in the month preceding the establishment of the subcommittee, there had been three major riots-at Laval Institute, at the B.C. penitentiary in my province and at Millhaven in the province of Ontario, in which a total of over $2 million damage had been done. A subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs was struck, which subcommittee, I might add, contained a number of very distinguished members of this House who are still members of the Elouse. I should particularly like to commend the work of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) who so ably chaired this subcommittee and who, I know, earned the respect not only of members of this House but of people all across Canada from the very many organizations involved in the field of corrections. He did an outstanding job and he deserves to be recognized for it once again by this House.
Hear, hear!

In addition, there were a number of distinguished lawyers on that committee, such as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who today is
958

November 5, 1979
Penitentiaries
chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and a number of other very distinguished members of this House. The hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) was a member of the subcommittee, as was the hon. member for Rosemount (Mr. Lachance) who is not in the House today. So was the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) and Mr. Stuart Leggatt who is not now a member of the House but is in Ottawa today. He played a very active role in the recommendations that led to the subcommittee report.
The subcommittee reported on May 26, 1977 with what might be considered record speed. It interviewed a large number of witnesses and travelled all across the country and to other parts of the world to examine penitentiary systems.
The subcommittee report, which I have before me, was a unanimous one. Members of the House will appreciate the significance of that. The report was perhaps an example of non-partisan politics at its finest. There was obviously some compromise but there was no question that the entire subcommittee unanimously supported the recommendations in the report. The key recommendation was No. 1 and 1 will read any excerpt from that into the record as follows:
A crisis exists in the Canadian penitentiary service. It can be met only by the immediate implementation of large scale reforms. It is imperative that the Solicitor General act immediately on this report as a matter of the utmost urgency.
That was in May, 1977. Unfortunately, the response of the then solicitor general was disturbing, to say the least. On this key recommendation with respect to a crisis existing in the penal system, a crisis detailed by a committee which had travelled from one side of the country to the other, the solicitor general, from the security of his office, said, "No, there is no crisis in the penal system; there may be problems, but crisis is perhaps not an appropriate word".
Things deteriorated from that point, Mr. Speaker. I might also add that during the period in which the subcommittee was making its investigation there was no violence whatsoever within the penal system. I think all components of the penal system had an air of expectation and had hoped that the subcommittee would come up with broad and sweeping recommendations for change, which, of course, it did.
Since that time, there have been a number of occasions both in committee and in the House where hon. members from all sides of the House have had an opportunity to monitor the implementation of the subcommittee's recommendations. It has been a rather sorry state of affairs.
I must again commend the former chairman of the subcommittee, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville, who despite the fact that he was a member of the government spoke out very articulately and forcefully, expressing his concerns about the failure of his government to implement a number of key recommendations of the subcommittee on penitentiaries. Certainly if his tones were strong, there was no question whatsoever where members of the Conservative party and members of my party stood on the recommendations of the subcommittee.
For example, in February this year, only a few short months ago, as a member of the opposition, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), now a member of the government, speaking on the motion for concurrence in the second report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, said as reported at page 2929 of Hansard:
We are as mad as hell, we are not going to take it any more, we are fed up with being ignored by the government.
He went on to talk about contempt. Later at page 2932 of Hansard he said:
What we are debating here today is this government's attitude to-one could almost say contempt for-parliament.
There was no doubt that members of the Conservative party who are now members of the government-the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the hon. member for St. John's East and a number of others, were very disturbed that the key recommendations of the subcommittee were not being implemented in areas such as ensuring an adequate scale of pay and recognition of working conditions within our penitentiary system. The fundamental concern was that those persons who work in such a penitentiary system be recognized as being basically in the front lines of what is a very arduous, difficult and demanding job. That has to be recognized not only in terms of pay, but in terms of pensions.
Surely it is wrong that the government should have to come before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and ask for supplementary estimates in order to give pensions to the widows and families of guards who are killed within the penitentiary system. What kind of recognition is that of the outstanding job being done by those persons who work within that system?
In addition, the subcommittee recommended that there should be voluntary retirement at age 55. Once again this recommendation has not been implemented by the government. In a moment I shall deal with the government's attitude toward implementation of the recommendations.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that we have to recognize the critical role that the staff within the penitentiary system plays. Morale has certainly not been high. There is no doubt about that. I have recently visited the B.C. penitentiary and a number of other institutions. There is no question that those persons who work in such institutions expected, and had every right to expect, that action would be taken, if nothing else at least on these critical recommendations with respect to working conditions within the penitentiary system.
In addition, the committee recommended in the strongest possible terms that there must be a separate, independent professional penitentiary staff system. This is very important, and it is a recommendation which to this date has again not been implemented by either the past or present government. There were concerns expressed about the size of our pentitenti-aries. There were concerns expressed about a number of different areas. In fact, what we saw was a gradual erosion of the number of recommendations stated to have been implemented by the government.

November 5, 1979

For example, on August 5, 1977, the then solicitor general, the present hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox) indicated that he had accepted 53 of the recommendations in whole or in part. In February, 1978 the solicitor general at that time said 37 of the recommendations had been implemented or were in the process of being implemented. In October, 1978, the then solicitor general talked about 22 recommendations that had been completely implemented.
Mr. Feggatt in his speech of February 6, 1979, indicated that it was his view that some 14 recommendations out of a total of 65 had in fact been implemented over a period, at that point, of one year and eight months since the subcommittee reported to the Flouse. I repeat, that-14 out of 65 recommendations had been implemented. The hon. member for Yukon, who is the present Minister of Public Works, in that same debate stated in no uncertain terms that his grievance was not with the solicitor general's department in terms of what it had done but in terms of what it had not done. He stated that the Liberals, Conservatives, members of the NDP and Social Credit parties had agreed unanimously, that this report ought to be taken as a package to be effective.
Its core recommendations have been completely ignored. He went on to say, 1 think quite rightly, that it is not irresponsible to suggest that unless something is done in a meaningful way about the adoption of the package of these recommendations, we will be back at square one. We all believed that this is what would happen when we submitted the report. To say we will be back at square one is a rather disturbing scenario, to say the least, if one bears in mind what I indicated square one was shortly before this subcommittee was established.
We have seen recently that one can build the finest institutions possible, where physical surroundings are flawless, and where living units are included etc. But where the basic recommendations of the subcommittee in terms of professionalization of staff and in terms of a number of other key recommendations, such as those relating to the grievance procedure, are not implemented, one can have the best institution in the world but we will still see flare-ups of the kind that took place at Kent institution within the past couple of weeks. In that case over half the prisoners were involved in a very expensive and damaging destruction of a substantial part of the Kent institution.
Where do we go from here, Mr. Speaker? We have a new government. We have members of this new government who have been active in opposition in calling for implementation, and full implementation, of the subcommittee's recommendations. As I said, we had the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) saying that they were fed up with the previous government's delay in implementing the recommendations, that they were not going to take it any more, and that they were fed up being ignored by the government.
These people are now members of the government. They now have an opportunity to implement those recommendations about which they were so concerned only a few short months ago. What do we see in response? Last week the Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence) appeared before the justice and legal
Penitentiaries
affairs committee with what he called a progress report. I have the document here. It concerns the implementation of the parliamentary report on the penitentiary system.
The present government has indicated that its view regarding implementation of these proposals is identical to that of the previous government. What kind of hypocrisy is this? What kind of charade are we being subjected to when, in opposition, members of this government, including a number of cabinet ministers, actively and outspokenly called for the implementation of the recommendations of the subcommittee? Yet when these people get into government and have a chance to implement the various recommendations, what happens? They are captured by the same bureaucracy, and we receive a report which might have been a photocopy of reports of January 1979, November 1978, March 1978, or August 1977. There is no change in the attitude of this government to the implementation of these recommendations.
I think that is a scandalous situation, Mr. Speaker. It is a scandalous situation when on the one hand the party in opposition can call in the strongest possible terms for the implementation of certain recommendations, yet when these people are in government and have a chance to act, what do they do? They carry on along the same course. It has been said by others, "progressive in opposition, conservative in government".
I want to say a word or two about the specific terms of this motion in the couple of moments I have left at my disposal. The motion calls for the establishment of a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which would be charged with the responsibility of examining the implementation of these recommendations. These were the recommendations which members opposite, now on the government side, were so concerned be implemented as a package. I say this subcommittee is essential, that there must be a body specifically charged with the responsibility of ensuring that these recommendations-all the recommendations, not just some of them-are implemented.
I understand that my friends on this side of the House will be supporting this motion. I would also hope that friends on the other side will not talk the motion out. 1 must say that I did speak with the Solicitor General, who indicated that he was prepared to accept the substance of this motion. He was prepared for there to be an ongoing permanent reference in line with recommendation 65 of the subcommittee, and he was prepared to appear, as he put it, whenever the committee asked him to appear with his officials. That is all well and good, but members opposite have a chance this afternoon to put their money where their mouth is and to allow this motion to come to a vote. It will be interesting to see whether, in that spirit of non-partisan debate which characterized the deliberations of the subcommittee, we will now be allowed to vote on this motion itself.
It is a straightforward motion. The recommendations of the subcommittee are clear. The attitudes of members opposite to those recommendations, and the failure to implement a number of them, have been clear for some time. I only hope

November 5, 1979
Penitentiaries
that that will be reflected in the vote taken today and that this motion will be passed unanimously by this House, just as the recommendations of the subcommittee were passed unanimously.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I say, I will await with interest the response of members on the other side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the motion put by the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). 1 am not going to take long because I want to make sure this motion has an opportunity of getting through. The last thing I want is to contribute to the talking out of a motion as important as this one. In fact, not only do we support this motion, but we have in effect made the same proposal ourselves.

The hon. member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) raised the question of implementation of recommendation 65 both in the House and in committee.

The most charitable thing to say about the response of the Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence) on both of those occasions was that he was evasive. He was evasive in the House, although he later claimed he misunderstood the question put in the House. We gave him a chance to put it right in committee but he was even more evasive. To indicate that this may even go beyond evasion, on the one hand he suggested that this recommendation was one of those which had been wholly accepted by the government. It was not on the list of those which had been rejected or was under question; it was on the list of those that had been accepted. Despite that assurance the Solicitor General said in committee that we do not need a reference of this kind, that we do not have time to deal with it, and that in any event it would be impossible to have this kind of reference. So much for his devotion to the implementation of recommendation 65.
Let us just take briefly each of those arguments. He says we do not need this kind of reference because of the fact that he is prepared to appear before us at any time. If we do not have a reference which enables us to hear him, how will he appear before us without a special order of reference? The House is well aware that the main estimates are due back in the House some time early in December. At that time the power of the committee to question the Solicitor General on this issue will expire, unless there is a special reference. It is a special reference we are talking about in this case.
He says we do not have time for it because we will have so much else to do in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. It is precisely because of this problem of time that we so strongly support the idea of a special reference. If that reference were to a subcommittee, if the subcommittee were a small one with one representative from each party, for example, the subcommittee could continue work on penitentiaries while the rest of the committee dealt with the work
before it. That would be a way of dividing the business before the committee and enabling it to do both things at once.
The argument the Solicitor General made actually turns back on himself. He attempted to argue procedure, that it is impossible to have a permanent reference. We were anticipating on the one hand that the government would some time soon make it possible to have permanent references to committees or even provide that they do not need orders of reference. This is supposed to be in the package of proposals which the government is going to be making to this House for the reform of the rules. It is one that meets with considerable favour on this side. If that is not the case, there is certainly the possibility of continuing orders of reference each session which achieve the same over-all purpose. It is splitting hairs to maintain it is not possible to give the committee these powers.
We on this side of the House have a suspicion that the implementation of this report by the correctional service is a largely nominal one. Not entirely, since there has been a lot of good implementation. But we were given a lot of statistics in the committee, a lot of things we did not have the opportunity to follow up. We have our suspicions about how deep implementations may be intended to go.
It is for this reason that we feel we need additional time to look at this problem. We simply cannot do the kind of job which this subject requires, we cannot do justice to the work of the subcommittee on penitentiaries which members on all sides of the House say they admire, unless we have the opportunity to continue it in detail in the future.
There is a lot more I would like to say about this subject. I would like to use this motion as a springboard to talk about penitentiaries and I am pleased the hon. member for Burnaby has given us this chance, but I will eschew the opportunity on this occasion. I want to hear whether the government is going to allow this motion to pass or whether instructions have been given to its supporters on the other side to talk it out.

Mr. Speaker, this is one of those topics where there seems to be little middle ground, and when one does speak out and take a stand, either one if viewed as believing penitentiaries should be like dungeons or that they should be like hotels and the prisoners the guests. Obviously, neither view is reality or what we as a society want our correctional service institutions to be. We as legislators must always be cognizant, even in the most serious and disturbing of times, that penitentiaries are there not because criminals are a bunch of mixed up kids. Criminals are there because they committed crimes, possibly violent crimes, and incarcerated only after due process of law and all its avenues have been exhausted. A prisoner or indeed anyone can be helped only if they want to be helped. Consideration and a want to help the inmate will only aid the rehabilitation process; it will not be the factor that will cause change.
The motion before this House today seeks to have a permanent reference during the Thirty-first Parliament to enable the House to review the implementation of the MacGuigan report. Certainly no one who believes that Parliament is important,

November 5, 1979

indeed the place where the laws of the land are made, could disagree in principle with this type of motion. Elowever, and I will speak further about this a little later, when there is good faith from a new minister and 51 of 65 recommendations are in process of implementation or shortly to be acted upon, and only five recommendations because of circumstances outside the control of the minister will not be acted upon, then I believe a motion to ask for a permanent reference to check their implementation is not only redundant but a waste of our time.

Why does he say it has been
implemented?

To answer the hon. member's question, the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) asked about and agreed with the terms of reference at the meeting last Thursday. Certainly until the private members' hour is changed, it does a disservice to the more important matters that could come before the House. 1 was pleased, however, to hear him mention the good work and results achieved by the committee.
1 concur with him in that regard. I had the opportunity to have a discussion with two former members, Mrs. Holt and John Reynolds, in Vancouver on Saturday night. They were not only more than pleased to have sat on that committee but pointed out the great work that had been done by the chairman of the committee. That is as far as 1 will go in support of the motion of the hon. member for Burnaby.
1 think it is worthwhile before looking at the report or the motion to look at the situation that caused these recommendations. The relative peace before 1970 ended in that year and between 1970 and 1976 the number of cases of hostage taking, violence and murders in the Canadian penitentiary system increased alarmingly. In the 42 years between 1932 and 1974 there were 65 major incidents in federal penitentiaries. Yet in the two years 1974-1976, before the subcommittee was struck, there were 69 incidents which included 33 hostage takings, 92 victims and one who was killed. The whole process of violence in federal institutions was not just increasing but rapidly accelerating. This situation was judged by the House of Commons to be unacceptable. The matter was referred to the justice and legal affairs committee which set up the subcommittee on the penitentiary system in Canada.
The situation had deteriorated so far that it just was not an intellectual argument of prisoners' rights or a simple matter of a few troublemakers. It was a question of credibility, credibility not only of the institution and the inmates but also of the institution and the general public. There was deep concern, and let us not forget this point, as to who was really running the institution in the minds of many average Canadians. The public could not be sure if the violence was the result of too much suppression and oppression from the security guards or because there was too little supervision and control being exerted.
With Canadians in that sort of quandary, action had to be taken to bring back some sense of order to the penitentiaries in
Penitentiaries
the minds of the citizens. The problem of credibility between the institution and the inmates was a totally different matter. Here it was not just a matter of perception or of public relations, but a question of intense frustration and anger at the lack of change in the institution. Mistrust had been allowed to developed which brought the inmates and staff to a state of anarchy. This whole attitude and situation reflected the state of the whole penitentiary system, not just one or two of the institutions.
The committee's work was intensive. It interviewed more than 2,000 inmates and staff, toured 24 institutes-seven of them outside Canada-and also held 72 formal meetings, lasting over 200 hours. The job done by the committee was just magnificent. The important thing about the 65 recommendations which came from this all-party subcommittee was that they were unanimously endorsed.
The recommendations covered a wide range of topics, from different types of rehabilitation to requirements for staff, to prisoner grievance procedures, to types of permissible treatment of prisoners, to reorganization of the system, and to new structure for the bureaucracy running institutions. The breadth of the recommendations, I think, represents the seriousness and the responsibility with which the sub-committee undertook in its task.
While one may have disagreements with any or all of the recommendations, it is an obvious fact that the 1970-1976 violence has definitely subsided. That is the important thing. Since that time only 17 hostage takings have occurred, which represents an over 60 per cent decrease just since the process started, therefore before any of the recommendations were implemented. The credibility of the system both in terms of the public and inmates has improved. Most Canadians today not only know who is running the correctional system but also feel that the rehabilitation process is much more effective than it was before 1976. Certainly with less violence one has to believe that the inmates have less outright hostility than they did prior to that time.
It is only natural in a penitentiary system that violence will occur from time to time. The important thing is that the violence which does occur is isolated and is associated with individual problems, not over-all grievances regarding the total correctional system. With the success of the sub-committee recommendations one would feel that on the whole they are moving the correctional service in the right direction.
However, to ask now as this motion does today for a permanent reference on the implementation of the recommendations is like shutting the barn door after the horses have bolted. The process of implementing the proposals is not starting but finishing, and not only is it finishing but it is doing it with a guarantee of co-operation from our new Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence). He is not ducking the issue, as the hon. member suggests or shirking his responsibility. On the contrary, the Solicitor General is being very open and, indeed,

November 5, 1979
Penitentiaries
very supportive of the wishes of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
This motion by the hon. member for Burnaby, while in principle acceptable, is really not needed. The hon. member knows that it is not needed, at least not at this point in time. The Solicitor General and, indeed, the two previous solicitors general have over the past two years regularly reported on the progress of the implementation of the report to the House. They have informed, as they should, the members of this House, the legislator of the land, of their department's action.
I listened to the Solicitor General last Thursday in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs detailing the remaining recommendations which have not as yet been acted upon. Of the remaining 14 recommendations, nine have been accepted in principle, and only five at this point in time will not be implemented. The reasons for the delay or the rejection of the recommendations were explained at that time. I cannot understand why the hon. member for Burnaby insisted on going through with this motion today. It is not a motion which threatens to implement any of the rejected recommendations but only asks this House for what is already taking place.
The frankness and the openness of the Solicitor General should be welcomed, not ignored, by this House. This motion rejects implicitly the reasons for not implementing the other five recommendations. The reasons range from jurisdictional problems to a belief by the minister that other, more appropriate changes have taken place and will suffice, and to where the Solicitor General feels he should remain responsible for his department and therefore, directly to Parliament, rather than shifting that responsibility to a committee which would report to him on the activities of the correctional services. Like many other programs in Canada's federalism, the recommendations will have to be negotiated by province.
To conclude and to reiterate, private members' hour is an important and valuable time period if used in the proper manner. This particular motion, in my opinion, is a useless occupation of hon. members' time in a parliamentary session which has much more to offer in terms of sensible legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in opposition to the motion, as did the last speaker. I regret that my address will not be as helpful to people who have not read the MacGuigan report as it will to people who have, but I will try to make it as clear as I can, bearing in mind that many people here probably have not read the MacGuigan report.
My remarks will deal with four aspects of the problem. First, I will review some of the events leading up to the MacGuigan report. Second, I will give some ideas on the penitentiary system. Third, I will discuss some of the principles underlying the recommendations in the MacGuigan report and the difficulties involved in maintaining a prison system. Fourth, I will give an indication of the progress of the implementation of some of the recommendations.
By way of background, between 1932 and 1974 a total of 65 major incidents occurred in Canadian penitentiaries. In 1975

and 1976 a total of 69 such incidents took place, including 35 hostage takings. This prompted the House of Commons to establish the sub-committee about which we have been talking today. That committee did very thorough work. It held 72 formal meetings. There were 407 witnesses. The committee conducted informal interviews with more than 2,000 inmates and staff. It toured seven U.S. institutions. The result of the inquiry was the MacGuigan report containing 65 recommendations.
The response of the government was an implementation committee which was established in the Department of the Solicitor General. To date, 51 of the 65 recommendations have been or are on the verge of being implemented. Five have been rejected, and nine are under review. The hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) and the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) were present the other day in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs when the new Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence) explained why at least some of those five were rejected.
A word about penitentiaries. "Penitentiaries" is an American term for an institution which was started in Philadelphia in about 1789 as a more humane alternative to the harsh punishment of the day.
Mir. Peters: What is the matter? Did you get the pages mixed up? That sounds like the beginning, not the middle of it. You should have come to that first.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The original idea was that penitentiaries, by offering isolation and opportunities for work, would provide an enlightening atmosphere, which would render people convicted of crimes penitent and reformed. The original reason for penitentiaries was a benevolent one, but unfortunately it did not work out that way.
Charles Dickens, after a visit to a penitentiary, wrote, and I will have to read this:
-I hold this slow and daily tampering with the mysteries of the brain to be immeasurably worse than any torture of the body; and because its ghastly signs are not so palpable to the eye-and it exhorts few cries that human ears can hear; therefore, I the more denounce it as a secret punishment which slumbering humanity is not roused up to stay.
November 5, 1979
That sounds like the NDP caucus.
I never saw you at one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Since Dickens' condemnation of the prison system, there has never been a time when the correctional system did not appear in need of rapid and substantial change. David Rothman, the historian, wrote the following:
Each generation discovers anew the scandals of incarceration, each sets out to correct them and each passes on a legacy of failure. The rallying cries of one period echo dismally into the next.
Actually, there has been a great deal of change in the last years, and prisons in Canada are very different now from the first Canadian penitentiary in Kingston in 1835. Large scale reform took place in 1960 as a result of MacLeod Committee's Correctional Planning Report. There were improved work programs, training and education were introduced, facilities were improved, new buildings were constructed. Two major changes were brought about: first, regional offices were established, and second, prison staff was unionized, becoming part of the Solicitor General's component of the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
If there is any inadequacy to my speech, Mr. Speaker, it is because of the flu from which I am suffering. I am afraid I have come from my sick bed this afternoon.
Don't be away tomorrow night.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The MacGuigan report argues that the two changes which 1 have just mentioned have led to a breakdown in authority, creating a confusion of roles and responsibilities which, when coupled with more militant inmate attitudes, have produced the violent upheavals that have been the chief characteristics in the 1970s.
Two important principles expounded in the MacGuigan report are: first, that the purposes of imprisonment are the protection of society and the denunciation of criminal behaviour. Imprisonment is a legitimate measure as a last resort where a wrongdoer, having been given the opportunity, has wilfully failed to comply with other, more constructive and less severe alternatives to imprisonment. Second, protection of society as a purpose of imprisonment includes not only protection during a term of imprisonment by the physical removal of a person who is dangerous or who has failed to respect values that are protected by the criminal law, but also the protection of society after his release by means of a prison system designed to assist him toward personal reformation.
These principles were fully accepted by the new Solicitor General who has expressed before the members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs the hope that the future attention of the committee will be focused on the provision of alternatives to incarceration.
Let me discuss these two principles in terms of the penitentiary system. In prison terms, protection of society means the collective control of violence. The MacGuigan report was undertaken with the understanding that the aim of prison
Penitentiaries
systems is the collective control of violence. In practice, the control of collective violence has been achieved by constant supervision and regimentation with elaborate systems of rules and regulations. In the past, some of these have gone to excesses. The maintenance of custody and order, the prevention of riots and escapes, have overshadowed every other consideration.
The MacGuigan report has properly recognized that to control collective violence, successfully, four conditions must be met: first, justice; second, alternatives to boredom; third, socialization; and fourth, good management.
The second principle refers to the idea of the prison system reforming the offender. The concept of rehabilitation is a fairly modern one which was not accepted in the past. Lor example, the last warden of New York's Sing-Sing prison believed that the aim of prison was to change inmates' behaviour rather than their character-to make them, if not better, at least more obedient to the criminal law. In his view, this was the only reform which society could expect.
In Canada the idea of rehabilitation arose in the 1950s in the Archambault and Lauteux reports, and stayed in the 1960s in the Ouimet report. It was to replace the "warehousing" approach which sought only to accomplish the task of keeping prisoners away from the public. The rehabilitation model caught on and was justified on humanitarian grounds and on the idea of transforming reformable criminals into law abiding citizens. But rehabilitation has proved to be a failure.
The MacGuigan report has also rejected this model. It believes that the incentive model is superior. It bases this on the principle that only the wrongdoer can bring about reform in himself, but the penitentiary system must be structured to give positive support to his efforts at reform by providing essential conditions. These conditions, as mentioned before, are: justice, work, and socialization.
Under the heading of justice, the condition of achieving justice in penitentiaries as stated in the MacGuigan report is based on three principles, which are, first, the sentence of imprisonment imposed by the court constitutes the punishment. People who work in the penitentiary system have no authority, right or duty to add to those penalties. Second, the rule of law must prevail inside Canadian penitentiaries, and third, justice for the inmate is a personal right and also an essential condition of their socialization and personal reformation. It implies both respect for the person and property of others and fairness in treatment. There must be clear rules, fair disciplinary procedures, and the provision of reasons for all decisions affecting inmates.
I cannot stress enough that these principles have all been accepted by the new Solicitor General. The rule of law is an axiom of common law. The concept that justice must prevail in every place and in every situation in Canada includes prisons. Indeed, someone has said that you can judge society not by what goes on outside prison walls but what goes on when someone has had liberty denied them. Where prisons are unjust, hatred is encouraged, and this ultimately leads to violence and the loss of control.

November 5, 1979
Penitentiaries
A number of steps have already been taken in the area of inmates' rights. First, as a result of recommendation No. 36 regarding inmate grievances, a new grievance procedure has been implemented which features speed in handling complaints, inmate involvement, and outside review. There is also a new system of a pre-grievance procedure. Second, in response to recommendation No. 29 which urged that the commissioner's directives be consolidated into a consistent code of regulations, a project was started to implement this recommendation. A project which involves rewriting the commissioner's directives that deal with the custody, treatment, training, employment and discipline of inmates, has also been begun and it should be operative by the spring of 1980. Also, all maximum and medium security institutions now have legal materials from which inmates can borrow on request.
I would like to say a word now on work and socialization. "Activity carries within itself the seeds of its own reformation", as was stated by Samuel Johnson. John Carlyle stated that "work is the grand cure of all maladies and miseries that ever beset mankind". Whether Carlyle and Johnson had prison in mind when they made these comments is certainly open to speculation, but these sentiments fit the second and third conditions in the MacGuigan report, that is, alternatives to boredom, and socialization, which the MacGuigan report believes are necessary.
The Solicitor General has assured the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs last Friday that, to his knowledge, every able and willing inmate is employed. Apparently, facilities for printing, audio-visual and microfilming now exist in several federal prisons. There is a new system of inmate pay, which is not at the rate that a lawyer or someone else might be paid, but it is being developed to provide an economic incentive to develop training skills. Farm production, kitchen gardening, horticultural programs, dairy and meat production are being increased.
Social interaction is another concern expressed by the MacGuigan report. According to the Solicitor General it is now a reality. 1 should like to give some examples. Common dining now has been established in nearly all institutions. Contact visiting has been made available. All inmates except those in dissociation and some in protective custody, of which I concede there are far too many, are now out of their cells for the greater part of the day and evening.
In response to the recommendations concerning socialization of inmates, new ideas such as the team concept, living unit and various treatment programs have been introduced into prisons. These are part of the concept of the incentive model recommended by the MacGuigan report. It goes without saying that his model is not necessarily popular with all inmates. The incentive model is based on the belief that the undesirable behaviour of others can be changed, even if this is done through somewhat coercive means. This coerced cure may be an advance in the prison system, as long as we keep in mind

the words of Norval Morris, director of the Centre for Studies in Criminal Justice at the University of Chicago. He said:
Rehabilitation, whatever it means and whatever the programs that allegedly give it meaning, must cease to be a purpose of the prison sanction. This does not mean that the various developed treatment programs within the prisons need to be abandoned; quite the contrary, they need expansion. But it does mean that they must not be seen as purposeful in the sense that criminals are to be sent to prison for treatment. There is a sharp distinction between the purpose of incarceration and the opportunities for the training and assistance of prisoners that may be pursued within those purposes. The system is corrupted when we fail to preserve this distinction and this failure pervades the world's prison programs.
I should like to make a comment on staff. Much of the MacGuigan report concerns itself with the inability of the staff of penitentiaries to function as a self-regulatory force to control the actions of a minority of offending guards who have contributed heavily to the atmosphere of confrontation in prisons. These negative impulses which affect the prisoner once incarcerated are the crux of the problem facing penitentiary services. The social problem has been at the root of the difficulties facing penal reform. The MacGuigan report succinctly points out, with regard to past programs of reform, that the changes which have occurred have failed to break down the core of repression upon which the system was built. With regard to this, and with reference to the correctional staff, the MacGuigan report sets forth principles five and six which read as follows:
(5)	Ways must be found to enlist the commitment, the reservoir of correctional expertise, the basic humanity and the capacity of the custodial staff to act as successful role-models for inmates in a co-operative effort to accomplish the great tasks that lie ahead of the Canadian Penitentiary Service.
(6)	A staff that is well-selected, well-motivated and well-paid is a key to any program of penitentiary reforms. Penitentiary work should be a professional career service modelled as far as practicable on the RCMP.
According to the MacGuigan report the incentive approach also should be applied to the staff. The idea of a professional attitude on the part of prison staff is stressed. I see the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville has returned to the chamber.
Just to hear the hon. member's comments.

He stated in a speech to the Canadian Association of Provincial Court Judges in Halifax:
Only professionalism can guarantee the existence of strong staff attitudes which will both prevent collective violence and offer the possibility of reformation of inmates.
The MacGuigan report lays particular stress on recommendation 26 which suggests the following:
. . . penitentiary service under the board must be an independent agency of the government and not subject to the Public Service Employment Act or the Public Service Staff Relations Act. It should resemble the RCM Police in its discipline and professionalism. Employees should be subject to discharge for misconduct or incompetence.
As expressed in the recommendation itself, the MacGuigan report had two reasons for this recommendation: the achievement of proper discipline among the employees, and the development of professionalism in the service.
The Solicitor General told the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs that a special task force has been developed to meet the recommendations dealing with the two reasons I have just mentioned. The primary objective of the
November 5, 1979

task force is to remove correctional service from the jurisdiction of the Public Service Employment Act. This will be achieved by referring to provisions in the Penitentiary Act which were rescinded by order in council in 1969. A schedule has been established for the continued work of the task force and the implementation of the recommendation involved. It is anticipated that by March, 1980, a new separate employer status will be created, along with the benefits which accrue to that status.
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
